title: Policy‐Guided Interregional Agricultural Cooperation Alters Water‐Energy‐Food Trade‐Offs in Cascade Reservoir Systems Under Climate Change
content:
Abstract

Climate change is altering precipitation, temperature, runoff, and crop water requirements, thereby changing both the availability and timing of water for irrigation and hydropower. In river basins regulated by multiple reservoirs, these changes can intensify competition between the two sectors, which depend on the same finite and seasonally variable water resources. Coordinated regional agricultural policies can shift irrigation water demand and thereby affect reservoir operation and water-energy-food trade-offs. This study develops a policy-to-operation framework that represents regional cooperation through combinations of agricultural-support levels and traces how the resulting demand changes affect WEF trade-offs through the joint operation of cascade reservoirs. The framework is applied to the Upper Yellow River Basin and its 23-reservoir system. Six agricultural support levels are assigned to each of four policy regions, resulting in 1,296 policy combinations evaluated under three CMIP6 SSPs in the near and far future. Raising agricultural support from the lowest to the highest level increases irrigation demand by approximately 37.1%, while reducing hydropower generation by 0.26%–1.15% and irrigation supply reliability by 2.15–4.89 percentage points in the near future. Policy effects are regionally asymmetric, with Gansu and Ningxia exerting the strongest influence on reservoir system outcomes. Nevertheless, 19.14%–37.58% of the configurations improve hydropower generation and irrigation supply reliability while reducing spill relative to the uniform medium support baseline, indicating that differentiated regional coordination can mitigate these conflicts. Preferred configurations vary across scenarios and periods, supporting differentiated and adaptive regional cooperation under climate change.
